477.title: The way to Brahma
477.hook: Subha asks about householder and renunciant; the four immeasurables as the way to Brahma
477.howItsDone: The four brahmavihāras, loving-kindness, compassion, appreciative joy and equanimity, are practiced across Buddhist traditions, often by radiating each one toward oneself, loved ones, strangers, difficult people and all beings in every direction.

segments.voice: Yesterday: preserving truth. Say this is my faith, not only this is true. Your line: preserve the truth. Now a new week.

A young brahmin named Subha is staying in Sāvatthī on business. He comes to the Buddha with a question that still turns up at kitchen tables. Who does better, the person who stays in the world, with a job and a family, or the person who leaves it all for a spiritual life? The brahmins of his day, he says, hold that the householder is the one who accomplishes what is good. What does the Buddha say? He answers by refusing to give a one-word answer.
screen: `SUBHA, IN TOWN ON BUSINESS.` → `THE HOUSEHOLDER OR THE ONE WHO LEAVES?` → `NO ONE-WORD ANSWER.`

segments.voice: On this, the Buddha says, I'm one who analyzes; I don't speak one-sidedly. A householder who lives badly doesn't accomplish the good, and neither does a monk who lives badly. A householder or a monk who lives well, either can. Then the talk turns to Brahmā, the high god the brahmins hoped to be united with after death. Subha has heard that the Buddha knows the way to companionship with Brahmā. The Buddha says: suppose a man was born and raised in a village called Naḷakāra, not far from here. If someone asked him the way to Naḷakāra, would he hesitate? No, he grew up there. In the same way, the Buddha says, I know Brahmā and the way there. So Subha asks: teach me the way. And the Buddha describes four states of heart. A person fills one direction with a mind of loving-kindness, then the second, the third, the fourth, then above, below, across, everywhere, a mind abundant, exalted, immeasurable, without hostility. Then compassion, the same way. Then appreciative joy, gladness at others' good. Then equanimity. These are the four immeasurables, also called the brahmavihāras, the dwellings of Brahmā. When the heart is freed like this, the Buddha says, no limited action remains there. And he gives a picture: a strong conch-blower makes himself heard in all four directions without effort. That's the way to Brahmā in this sutta: not a ritual, not a birth, but a heart grown so wide it has no edges. Subha leaves delighted, and goes for refuge.

segments.voice: Choose one immeasurable, kindness, compassion, gladness at others' good, or steady equanimity, and feel it first toward someone easy. Then let it spread the way the sutta says, in front of you, behind, to the sides, above and below, until it has no edge. If your mind wanders, start again with the easy person.
Brahmavihara. Loving-kindness, compassion, appreciative joy and equanimity, spread in every direction without limit: the dwellings of Brahmā.
Your line: a heart with no edges. Like a conch heard in all four directions. Until tomorrow.

478.title: The arrow-maker's fire
478.hook: at Devadaha: the fletcher warms the arrow to straighten it, then stops; effort without self-torment
478.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers often describe the path as a middle way between indulgence and self-torment, and encourage steady, balanced effort in meditation rather than forcing.

segments.voice: Yesterday: brahmavihara, the four immeasurables spread in every direction. Your line: a heart with no edges.

There are two ways to get nowhere with self-improvement. One is to never try. The other is to try so hard you punish yourself: the 5am alarm you hate, the diet that makes you miserable, the inner voice that never says well done. The Buddha knew the second way well. Before his awakening, the old stories say, he starved himself until he was skin and bone. In a Sakyan town called Devadaha, he talks about effort, and he reaches for a picture from a craftsman's workshop.
screen: `NEVER TRYING.` → `TRYING UNTIL IT HURTS.` → `A CRAFTSMAN'S WORKSHOP.`

segments.voice: The sutta opens with a debate about ascetics of the time who held that painful austerities burn away past actions. The Buddha questions that view at length. Then he describes what fruitful effort looks like. A monk, he says, doesn't overwhelm himself with suffering. He doesn't reject a pleasure that's in line with the teaching, and he isn't infatuated with it either. Then the picture. An arrow-maker has a crooked arrow shaft. He warms it between two flames, turning it, heating it, bending it until it's straight and workable. And once it's straight? He stops. He doesn't keep heating a straight arrow; the purpose is done. In the same way, the Buddha says, a person might notice: when I live just as I please, unwholesome things grow in me; when I put in some hard effort, they fade. So they apply the heat, as much as is needed, and when the purpose is achieved, they stop. Heat has a job: straightening. Harm has no job. Self-punishment that goes on after the arrow is straight isn't discipline. It's just burning. The Dhammapada uses the same craftsman. In Max Müller's words: "As a fletcher makes straight his arrow, a wise man makes straight his trembling and unsteady thought, which is difficult to guard, difficult to hold back." The fletcher isn't angry at the wood. He's patient with it, and he knows when to put the arrow down.

segments.voice: Think of one thing in yourself you're working to straighten, a temper, a habit, a way of speaking, and notice how you usually talk to yourself about it: is it heat, or harm? Picture the fletcher warming the shaft gently, turning it, checking it, and bring that tone to your own effort. Then rest with the breath, and let the heat go out.
Usukara. The fletcher heats a crooked shaft until it's straight, and then stops. Effort with a purpose, without self-torment.
Your line: heat, not harm. Once the arrow is straight, the heat has done its job. Day four hundred seventy-eight.

479.title: Meaning, not wording
479.hook: settling disagreements about the letter versus the meaning
479.howItsDone: Buddhist communities across the world chant and study the teachings in many languages and translations, and some teachers point to this sutta to explain why the meaning matters more than identical wording.

segments.voice: Yesterday: usukara, the arrow-maker who heats a crooked shaft until it's straight, then stops. Your line was heat, not harm.

Two friends are arguing in a group chat. One says the meeting is at half past. The other says no, thirty minutes past. Ten messages in, someone points out they're saying the same thing. Real disagreements are rarely that silly, but some turn out to be about the words, not the thing. In a grove near the town of Kusinārā, the Buddha gives the monks a short talk on exactly this: what to do when the community disagrees about the teaching itself.
screen: `HALF PAST, OR THIRTY MINUTES PAST?` → `THE SAME THING, TEN MESSAGES IN.` → `KUSINĀRĀ.`

segments.voice: He starts by reminding them what he's taught: the foundations of mindfulness, the right efforts, the factors of awakening, the noble path. Train in these in harmony, he says, without quarreling. Then he's realistic. Disputes will happen, so he sorts them. Pali has two words here: attha, the meaning, and byañjana, the wording, literally the letters. Suppose two monks differ about both the meaning and the wording. Then someone should go to the more approachable one and say gently: you differ about the meaning and the wording; please don't fall into a quarrel. Then the same with the other. If they differ about the meaning but agree on the wording, same approach: point it out, and keep the peace. But if they agree about the meaning and differ only about the wording, the Buddha says, the wording is a trifle. Don't fall into a quarrel over a trifle. That's the heart of it. When people share what something means, the exact words are small. The sutta then turns to correcting someone who has done wrong: don't rush; think first whether it will help, whether the person will listen, whether you can do it without distress. If it can be done kindly, do it. On an ordinary day, this saves a lot of grief. Before arguing, ask: do we disagree about what this means, or only about how to say it?

segments.voice: Bring to mind a recent disagreement, at home, at work or online, and replay it slowly. Ask what the other person meant, what you meant, and whether those were really different or you were fighting over a word. If the meanings were close, picture saying so, I think we mean the same thing, and let your shoulders drop.
Meaning. Attha, what a teaching means, set beside byañjana, the wording. When the meaning is shared, the Buddha calls the wording a trifle.
Your line: don't quarrel over a trifle. When the meaning is shared, the words are small. See you tomorrow.

480.title: Settling disputes
480.hook: after a teacher's death disputes arise; seven ways of settling them
480.howItsDone: The seven ways of settling disputes (adhikaraṇa-samatha) are part of the monastic code recited at the fortnightly Pāṭimokkha ceremony, and monastic communities still use them, including 'covering over with grass', to resolve conflicts.

segments.voice: Yesterday: attha, the meaning, set beside the wording. Your line was don't quarrel over a trifle.

A young novice named Cunda has spent the rains in the town of Pāvā, and he walks in with bad news. A well-known teacher of the time has just died there, and his followers are already splitting into camps, wounding each other with words: you don't understand the teaching; I do. Cunda tells Ānanda, and Ānanda takes him straight to the Buddha. Ānanda is worried. When you're gone, he asks, could this happen to us?
screen: `CUNDA, BACK FROM PĀVĀ.` → `A TEACHER DIES. HIS FOLLOWERS SPLIT.` → `COULD THIS HAPPEN TO US?`

segments.voice: The Buddha's answer is reassuring and sharp at once. Disputes about small things, how monks earn their keep, details of the monastic rules, those are minor, Ānanda. A dispute about the path itself would be serious, and would harm many. Then he lays out how to settle the disputes that will come. The Pali word for a dispute is adhikaraṇa, and the sutta gives seven ways to settle one. Some you'd expect: face to face, with the people, the teaching and the rules all present; by majority vote, when nothing else works; by someone's own admission of what they did. Some are surprisingly humane. One clears a monk accused of something he did while out of his mind: he's not held responsible. One clears a monk with a clear memory and a clean record, so false accusations don't stick. And the last has a striking name: covering over with grass. When a whole community is tangled in a long, messy quarrel, with faults on every side, and digging it all up would only make things worse, both sides agree to set it aside together, like covering mud with grass so people can walk again. Serious offenses are excluded. For the rest, peace is allowed to matter more than a full accounting. Then six qualities that keep a community warm: kindness in body, speech and mind, sharing what you receive, the same good conduct, and the same understanding. Disputes will come; a community can be built to settle them.
screen: `SMALL DISPUTES, AND SERIOUS ONES.` · `FACE TO FACE, BY VOTE, BY ADMISSION.` · `CLEARED BY MEMORY, OR BY PAST MADNESS.` · `COVERING OVER WITH GRASS.` · then, large: `SETTLE IT.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one small, ongoing friction: whose turn it is, a comment that stung, an old disagreement that keeps resurfacing. Ask which of the seven ways might fit: face to face, an honest admission, or covering it over with grass, agreeing together to let it rest. Picture the first sentence you'd say, then rest with the breath.
Settling disputes. The seven ways the Buddha gave his community, from face to face to covering over with grass, so a quarrel doesn't outlive its cause.
Your line: settle it. Even a long quarrel can be covered with grass. Day four hundred eighty, done.

481.title: I only show the way
481.hook: the gradual training, like an accountant's method; some arrive, some don't; I only show the way
481.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers commonly describe themselves as guides rather than saviors, and students are taught the path in stages, from keeping precepts to guarding the senses, mindfulness and meditation.

segments.voice: Yesterday: seven ways of settling disputes, down to covering over with grass. Your line was settle it.

Moggallāna the accountant, a brahmin, not the famous monk of the same name, is visiting the Buddha at a palace-monastery in Sāvatthī. He notices the staircase. In this building, he says, you can see a gradual progress, step by step, all the way to the top stair. Our brahmin studies are like that. So is archery. And in my trade, accounting, we teach a student to count step by step: one, two, three, on up to a hundred. Is there anything like that in your teaching?
screen: `MOGGALLĀNA THE ACCOUNTANT.` → `A STAIRCASE, STEP BY STEP.` → `ONE, TWO, THREE, UP TO A HUNDRED.`

segments.voice: There is, says the Buddha. Like a skilled horse trainer with a fine colt, I start a person with the first step: live by the precepts, see the danger in small faults. Then guard the senses: when you see a shape, don't grab at it. Eat in moderation, not for fun or show, just enough to keep the body going. Be wakeful, walking and sitting by day and in the early night. Be mindful in everything, going out and coming back, eating, dressing, speaking, keeping silent. Then a quiet place, a forest or the foot of a tree, the body upright, the hindrances let go, and deep stillness, one stage after another. Then Moggallāna asks the harder question. Does everyone you teach reach the goal? No, the Buddha says. Some do, some don't. Why not, if the path is there and you're there to guide it? Suppose someone asks you the way to Rājagaha. You tell them clearly: go this way, you'll see a village, then a town, then Rājagaha itself, with its parks and ponds. One person follows the directions and arrives. Another takes the wrong road. Whose fault is that? The city is there. The road is there. You were there to point. And the Buddha says: the Tathāgata only shows the way. The Dhammapada says it in Max Müller's words: "You yourself must make an effort. The Tathâgatas (Buddhas) are only preachers."
screen: `THE FIRST STEP: THE PRECEPTS.` · `SENSES, MODERATION, WAKEFULNESS, MINDFULNESS.` · `DOES EVERYONE ARRIVE? NO.` · `THE ROAD TO RĀJAGAHA.` · then, large: `I ONLY SHOW THE WAY.`

segments.voice: Picture whatever path you're on as a road with landmarks, and see where you are now: by the village, or the town. Don't measure how far it is to the city; just see the next small step, a precept kept more carefully, a meal eaten mindfully, a little longer sitting, and breathe with it.
Tathagata, the Buddha's word for himself as one who only shows the way. The gradual training is there, step by step like counting, but the walking is up to each person.
Your line: the walking is yours. The teacher points, and the road stays open. That's day four eighty-one.

482.title: The teaching is the refuge
482.hook: after the Buddha's death Ananda says the dhamma is their refuge
482.howItsDone: Theravada monastic communities recite the Patimokkha, the training code, together on the new-moon and full-moon observance days, and seniority and respect within the community rest on ordination and conduct rather than on a single appointed leader of the whole tradition.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the accountant's step-by-step training, and your line, the walking is yours.

When a founder dies, one question comes fast: who's in charge now? Bands face it, and family businesses. The hundred and eighth discourse of the Middle-Length Sayings is set just after the Buddha's death. Ananda, his attendant, is in the city of Rajagaha. The kingdom is nervous; the city's walls are being strengthened against a rival king. And a powerful minister named Vassakara comes to ask Ananda exactly that question. Who leads you now?
screen: `WHO'S IN CHARGE NOW?` → `RAJAGAHA, JUST AFTER THE BUDDHA'S DEATH.` → `A MINISTER ASKS ANANDA.`

segments.voice: It starts with a smaller question. Ananda visits a brahmin named Gopaka Moggallana at a building site. Is there any monk, Gopaka asks, who has every quality the Buddha had? No, says Ananda. The Buddha found a path that wasn't known; his students only follow it. Then Vassakara arrives and presses harder. Did the Buddha appoint a monk to be your refuge after him? No. Did the community choose one? No. Then you have no refuge. So what keeps you together? Ananda turns the question around. We are not without a refuge, he says. The teaching is our refuge. Then he gets practical. There's a training code, recited together on the moon days. Whoever has slipped says so, and the group handles it by the teaching, not by anyone's favor. No monk gives the orders; the teaching does. That doesn't mean nobody is respected. Yes, Ananda says, they honor certain monks, but for what they live: virtue, learning, contentment, stillness and insight. Respect follows the practice, not a title. This fits what the Buddha said near the end of his life, in another discourse: be islands to yourselves, with the teaching as your refuge. Ananda isn't improvising; he's doing what he was told. Monastic communities still gather to recite a shared code together. When the founder is gone, the refuge is what he left in their hands.
screen: `NO ONE HAS ALL HIS QUALITIES` · `NO APPOINTED HEIR` · `THE TEACHING IS OUR REFUGE` · `RESPECT FOLLOWS PRACTICE` · then, large: `THE TEACHING IS THE REFUGE.`

segments.voice: Let the breath arrive on its own, and bring to mind one teaching from this year that has stayed with you, a line, a simile, a story. 483.title: The full-moon night
483.hook: on a full-moon night a monk asks about the five heaps
483.howItsDone: In many Buddhist countries the full-moon observance day (uposatha, or poya in Sri Lanka) is when lay people visit temples, keep extra precepts and hear teachings, and monastics gather to recite their training code.

segments.voice: Yesterday: no appointed heir, and your line, respect follows the practice. Today closes a week.

Some conversations only happen outside, at night. Phones down, a porch or a rooftop, the moon bright enough to see faces. People ask things there they'd never ask at noon. The hundred and ninth discourse happens on a night like that: the observance day of the fifteenth, the full moon. The Buddha sits in the open air at the Eastern Park near Savatthi, the monks around him. One monk stands, arranges his robe over one shoulder, and asks if he may put a question. He has more than one.
screen: `QUESTIONS PEOPLE ONLY ASK AT NIGHT` → `THE FIFTEENTH. THE FULL MOON.` → `ONE MONK STANDS UP.`

segments.voice: His questions are all about the five heaps, the khandhas: body, feeling, perception, mental formations and consciousness, the bundles a person seems to be made of. Are these the five heaps we cling to? Yes. What are they rooted in? Desire. Then a sharp one: is the clinging the same as the heaps, or apart from them? Neither, the Buddha says. The clinging is the desire and lust for them. The heaps are just heaps; the trouble is the grabbing. Why call them heaps? Because each gathers everything of its kind: past, future and present, near and far, coarse and subtle. Body rests on the four elements. Feeling, perception and formations rest on contact. Consciousness rests on name-and-form. And a sense of self gets built by taking any heap as me, or mine, or my self. Then a twist. Another monk has a quiet worry: if there's no self, who receives the results of my deeds? The Buddha knows the thought. He warns that someone driven by craving might try to outrun the teaching this way, then turns it back into questions. Is body permanent or impermanent? Impermanent. Is what's impermanent worth calling me? No. The text closes saying that as he spoke, sixty monks were freed. Look back at the week: a way to Brahma through boundless kindness, an arrow-maker's warmth, meaning over wording, disputes settled, a path shown, a teaching for refuge. And now the five heaps, under a full moon.
screen: `FIVE HEAPS, ROOTED IN DESIRE` · `THE CLINGING IS THE GRABBING` · `WHO RECEIVES THE DEEDS?` · `SIXTY MONKS FREED` · then, large: `THE FULL-MOON NIGHT.`

segments.voice: Picture an open night sky, and look lightly for the five heaps in yourself: a body sitting, a feeling pleasant or not, a sound you're naming, a small intention forming, and knowing underneath it all. Don't grab any of them; let them be heaps under a wide sky.
Khandhas. The five heaps, body, feeling, perception, formations and consciousness, that a monk asked the Buddha about on the full-moon night, learning the clinging is the grabbing, not the heaps.
Your line: the clinging is the grabbing. The heaps are only heaps. That's the week.
